claims.text: The patient presented on 2026-01-07 with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and the worst headache of her life, associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, fever, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
Past medical history was recorded as nil, with no current medications and no known allergies documented at presentation.

Social history includes living alone, independence in daily activities, working as a primary school teacher, no smoking or recreational drug use, moderate alcohol consumption (approximately 6 units per week), and regular jogging.
Family history reported no immediate family history of CVA, aneurysms, migraines, or neurological conditions, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.
Initial observations on 2026-01-07 at 14:05 and 14:20 showed blood pressure 160/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7-36.8°C, and SpO2 98% on room air.
Initial neurological examination on 2026-01-07 revealed no focal deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, normal reflexes, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
CT head scan performed on 2026-01-07 at 14:45 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormalities.
Blood tests collected on 2026-01-07 at 15:15 showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP 8 mg/L, normal renal function, and normal liver function tests.
An initial diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) was made in the Emergency Department on 2026-01-07 based on clinical presentation and CT findings.
On 2026-01-07, treatment was initiated with oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for suspected RCVS.
On 2026-01-07, blood results indicated mild hypokalemia with potassium 3.3 mmol/L.
On 2026-01-07, potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily was prescribed to correct hypokalemia.
On 2026-01-07, the patient's headache severity was recorded as 7/10 with blood pressure elevated at 150/92 mmHg.
MRI/MRA of the brain and cerebral vasculature arranged on 2026-01-07 confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS on 2026-01-08.
On 2026-01-08, the patient reported a reduction in headache severity to 5/10, with blood pressure recorded at 135/85 mmHg and CRP at 12 mg/L.
On 2026-01-08, the nimodipine regimen was changed to 30 mg orally every 4 hours.
On 2026-01-08, blood tests revealed mild hyponatremia with sodium 132 mmol/L.
On 2026-01-09, the patient reported a marked reduction in headache severity to 3/10, with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm.
Management for hyponatremia on 2026-01-09 included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures and restricting excessive fluid intake.
On 2026-01-09, a repeat MRA was planned for 24 hours later to assess resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-10, the patient reported significant improvement in headache to 2/10 intensity, with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg and heart rate 78 bpm.
On 2026-01-10, a repeat MRA was planned for 2026-01-11 to assess resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-11 at 10:30, a repeat MRA demonstrated significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-11, observations showed blood pressure 125/78 mmHg and heart rate 72 bpm.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches and felt well, with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm.
On 2026-01-12, a repeat MRA performed on 2026-01-11 was confirmed to show resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-12, the discharge plan included tapering oral nimodipine 30 mg four times daily over two weeks.

On 2026-01-12, a medication discrepancy exists regarding the discharge regimen: one source states the plan is to taper nimodipine 30 mg QDS, while another source states the discharge medication discussed with the GP was amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
On 2026-01-12, the patient was discharged home with a referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks.

Patient education provided included materials on RCVS, avoidance of triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines, and a discharge planning booklet reviewed on 2026-01-10 and 2026-01-12.

Rehabilitation assessment on 2026-01-09 noted mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, with a decision to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge and no inpatient sessions required.
The patient's GP, Dr. Ethel Joanne Duffy, was contacted on 2026-01-07 at 20:00 and again on 2026-01-12 at 12:00 to provide updates on admission, diagnosis, and discharge.
